en.title: Statistics: the whole course
en.short: What statistics covers, how statistics degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What statistics is
sections.text:
Statistics is the science of collecting data, describing it, and drawing conclusions from it under uncertainty. It gives you tools to measure how much of a result could be due to chance, and to say honestly how confident you can be.

The subject has two sides that support each other. One is the mathematics of probability and inference. The other is the practical work of designing a study, cleaning data, choosing a method and explaining what the numbers mean.

Statistics matters because decisions in medicine, farming, business and government are made from incomplete information. A well-trained statistician says clearly what the data can and cannot support.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and by institution, so check your own student handbook rather than relying on a general description.

In Nigeria a BSc in statistics usually takes four years at a university, with the later years concentrating on statistical methods. Polytechnic students usually take an ND and then an HND, with a period of supervised industrial work between them. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland a BSc usually takes three years and an integrated master’s four, while in Scotland each is often a year longer. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa have their own structures.

Most programmes mix lectures with practical classes in a computer laboratory, and end with a project or dissertation. A master’s degree adds advanced theory, statistical learning and a research dissertation. Professional bodies, such as the Nigerian Statistical Association, exist in many countries; their membership rules change, so check the current requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics come first. Mathematical foundations covers the algebra, calculus and matrix ideas you will use. Data, variables and study design covers types of data, sampling, and the difference between experiments and observational studies. Descriptive statistics covers summaries, tables and graphs. Probability foundations and random variables lead to the standard distributions.

Then come the ideas that make inference possible: sampling distributions and the central limit theorem, estimation and confidence intervals, and the principles of hypothesis testing. Correlation and simple linear regression, and the analysis of contingency tables with chi-square tests, complete the introductory stage.

The core stage widens the toolkit: multiple regression, analysis of variance, design of experiments, logistic and log-linear models, nonparametric methods, multivariate analysis, time series, survey sampling, statistical quality control, stochastic processes, Bayesian inference, statistical computing, survival analysis, causal inference from observational studies, the theory of estimation and testing, and professional practice and ethics.

At master’s level come advanced inference, statistical learning, hierarchical and mixed-effects models, and research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work through the mathematics with pen and paper. Reading a proof or a worked example is not the same as being able to reproduce it, and the algebra in statistics is where many marks are lost.

Do the arithmetic in examples yourself before reading the answer, then compare. Ask whether the result is plausible: a probability outside 0 and 1, or a confidence interval that does not contain the estimate, signals an error.

Use a computer from early on. Learn one package well, such as R, Python or Stata, but always check output against a small hand calculation. Keep a notebook of definitions and formulas, and write down the conditions under which each method is valid. Practise interpreting results in plain words, because that is what employers and examiners ask for.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Statistics is the science of collecting data, describing it, and drawing conclusions under uncertainty.
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from probability and descriptive tools to inference, then to modelling and advanced methods.
Do the algebra and the arithmetic yourself; reading a worked solution is not the same as being able to produce one.
Check that every method’s assumptions hold before you use it.
A p value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and correlation is not causation.

en.title: Mathematical foundations for statistics
en.short: Summation, functions, logs and exponentials, derivatives and integrals, and matrix operations for statistics.

sections.heading: Summation and functions
sections.text:
Summation notation Σ is shorthand for adding terms. Σ from i = 1 to n of x_i means x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_n. For x = (1, 2, 3, 4), Σ x_i² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30.

A function f maps each input x to one output f(x); for f(x) = 2x + 1, f(3) = 7. Its domain is the set of allowed inputs.

sections.heading: Logs and exponentials
sections.text:
Logarithms undo exponentials. If b^y = x, then log_b x = y, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1. Rules include log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y and log_b(x^a) = a log_b x. The natural logarithm ln has base e ≈ 2.718.

For example, log_10(1000) = 3 and ln(e²) = 2. Logs turn products into sums and help with likelihoods and skewed data.

sections.heading: Derivatives and integrals
sections.text:
A derivative gives the rate of change of a function. For f(x) = x^n, f'(x) = n x^(n−1). For f(x) = 3x², f'(x) = 6x, so at x = 2 the slope is 12.

An integral accumulates area. For n ≠ −1, ∫ x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx = [x³] from 0 to 2 = 8. Derivatives locate likelihood maxima; integrals give probabilities as areas under densities.

sections.heading: Matrix operations
sections.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array. If A is m × n and B is n × p, AB is m × p; entry (i,j) is the sum of A(i,k)B(k,j) over k. For A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[2,0],[1,1]], AB = [[4,2],[10,4]]. The transpose A' swaps rows and columns.

For [[a,b],[c,d]], the determinant is ad − bc; here det A = 1×4 − 2×3 = −2. If det A ≠ 0, A has an inverse A⁻¹ with A A⁻¹ = I. Statistics uses matrices for data, covariance and normal equations.

keyPoints: Σ from i = 1 to n of x_i adds the n values; for x = (1, 2, 3, 4), Σ x_i² = 30.
A function f maps each input to one output; f(x) = 2x + 1 gives f(3) = 7.
Log rules: log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y and log_b(x^a) = a log_b x; ln(e²) = 2.
Derivative of x^n is n x^(n−1); integral of x^n is x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n ≠ −1.
An inverse A⁻¹ exists when det A ≠ 0 and satisfies A A⁻¹ = I.

en.title: Data, variables and study design
en.short: Variable types, measurement scales, sampling methods, experiments, bias and confounding.

sections.heading: Variables and scales
sections.text:
A variable is a characteristic that differs between units. Categorical variables record labels; quantitative variables record numbers. Quantitative variables are discrete if countable, or continuous if they take any value in a range.

Nominal data are unordered labels, such as blood group. Ordinal data have order but unequal gaps, such as pain rated mild, moderate or severe. Interval data have equal gaps but no true zero, such as temperature in °C. Ratio data have equal gaps and a true zero, such as mass. Only ratio data support twice as much.

sections.heading: Populations and samples
sections.text:
A population is the whole set you want to describe; a sample is the part you study. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. It should cover the population; if it leaves groups out, the sample may not represent them.

Example: a department register of 120 students is a frame; 20 chosen by random numbers form a simple random sample. A statistic from the sample estimates the population parameter.

sections.heading: Sampling methods
sections.text:
In simple random sampling every unit and every combination of the required size has an equal chance of selection. It is the basic method.

Stratified sampling divides the population into strata, such as year of study, then samples randomly within each stratum. It can improve precision when strata differ.

Cluster sampling selects whole groups, such as classes or villages, then studies all or a random subset. It helps when no individual list exists, but cluster members may be alike, so estimates are less precise.

sections.heading: Bias and design
sections.text:
An observational study records units without controlling treatment. An experiment assigns treatments, so it can support cause and effect when properly randomised.

Bias is a systematic error pushing results one way. Sources include an incomplete frame, non-response and poor questions. Confounding occurs when a third variable is linked to both exposure and outcome, so the apparent association is distorted. Randomisation balances confounders; observational studies must measure and adjust for them.

keyPoints: Categorical variables are labels; quantitative variables are numbers, either discrete or continuous.
Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales differ in order, equal gaps and true zero.
A population is the whole set; a sample is part of it, drawn from a sampling frame.
Simple random sampling gives equal chances; stratified sampling samples within strata; cluster sampling selects whole groups.
Observational studies record without assigning treatment; experiments assign treatments and can support cause and effect when randomised.
Bias is systematic error; confounding is a third variable linked to both exposure and outcome.

en.title: Descriptive statistics: tables, graphs and z-scores
en.short: Frequency tables and graphs, centre and spread, boxplots and outliers, and z-scores.

sections.heading: Frequency tables and graphs
sections.text:
Raw data are hard to read, so group them. A frequency table lists classes (intervals), midpoints, and the count in each class (frequency). Relative frequency is frequency ÷ total. Cumulative frequency adds frequencies up to a class.

For continuous data, draw a histogram: bars touch, and area represents frequency. For categories, use a bar chart with gaps. A frequency polygon joins class midpoints; an ogive plots cumulative frequency. Choose class width to show patterns without too much detail.

sections.heading: Centre, spread and shape
sections.text:
Measures of centre: mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle value when ordered; mode is the most frequent value. Spread: range = max − min; interquartile range IQR = Q3 − Q1; sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1), and standard deviation s = √s². Use n for a population.

Shape: a symmetric distribution has mean roughly equal to median; right-skewed has a long right tail and usually mean > median; left-skewed has mean < median. The mean is affected by outliers; the median is resistant.

sections.heading: Five-number summary and boxplots
sections.text:
The five-number summary is minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. Quartile definitions vary slightly. A boxplot draws a box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median; whiskers reach the most extreme values that are not outliers.

A common rule flags values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR as outliers. State the rule you use. Boxplots compare groups quickly.

sections.heading: Standardisation and z-scores
sections.text:
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: z = (x − x̄) ÷ s. Standardising a set gives mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

Example: for 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, x̄ = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 and s² = 28 ÷ 4 = 7, so s = 2.65. For x = 9, z = (9 − 5) ÷ 2.65 = 1.51, so 9 is 1.51 standard deviations above the mean. z-scores compare values from different scales.

keyPoints: A frequency table groups values into classes; a histogram shows continuous frequencies with touching bars.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent value.
Sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1); standard deviation s = √s².
IQR = Q3 − Q1; a common outlier rule is outside Q1 − 1.5×IQR or Q3 + 1.5×IQR.
The five-number summary is minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
A z-score is z = (x − x̄) ÷ s; it counts standard deviations from the mean.

en.title: Probability foundations
en.short: Covers sample spaces, axioms, conditional probability, independence, Bayes’ theorem and counting rules.

sections.heading: Sample spaces
sections.text: An experiment is any process with an uncertain result. Its sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of S. For a fair die, S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. The event A = {2,4,6} means an even score, so P(A) = 3 ÷ 6 = 1/2. Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together, so their intersection is empty.

sections.heading: Axioms
sections.text: Probability assigns P(A) to each event A. The axioms are: P(A) ≥ 0; P(S) = 1; and for disjoint events A and B, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). From these come P(no outcome) = 0 and P(not A) = 1 − P(A). For any two events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

sections.heading: Conditional and Bayes
sections.text: Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B), for P(B) > 0. It rescales the sample space to B. Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), which gives P(A | B) = P(A). Bayes’ theorem reverses a conditional: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A) ÷ P(B). Example: a disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test is positive in 99% of cases and in 5% of healthy people. P(disease | positive) = (0.01 × 0.99) ÷ (0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05) = 0.0099 ÷ 0.0594 = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. So about 16.7% of positive tests are true cases.

sections.heading: Counting
sections.text: The multiplication rule says that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, the pair can be made in m × n ways. Permutations count ordered arrangements: nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!, where n! = n × (n − 1) × ... × 1. Combinations count unordered selections: nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Example: choosing 2 students from 5 gives 5C2 = 5! ÷ (2! × 3!) = 10 groups.

keyPoints: Sample space S is the set of all outcomes; an event is a subset of S.
Axioms: P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) for disjoint A and B.
Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B), with P(B) > 0.
Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); Bayes’ theorem is P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A) ÷ P(B).
Counting: multiplication m × n; permutations n! ÷ (n − r)!; combinations n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!).
Check that every probability lies between 0 and 1 and that conditional probability uses the reduced sample space.

en.title: Random variables and probability distributions
en.short: Discrete and continuous variables, pmf, pdf, cdf, expectation, variance and five common distributions.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text:
A random variable is a rule that assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. A discrete random variable takes countable values, such as the number of defective items in a sample.

A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, such as waiting time. Its probability at an exact point is zero; probabilities come from intervals. A distribution tells how probability is spread over the possible values.

sections.heading: Mass, density and cdf
sections.text:
For a discrete variable, the probability mass function gives p(x) = P(X = x); probabilities are non-negative and sum to 1. For a continuous variable, the probability density function f(x) gives probability by area: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the area under f from a to b, and the total area is 1.

The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It rises from 0 to 1; for discrete variables it is a step function, and for continuous variables it is the integral of f up to x.

sections.heading: Expectation and variance
sections.text:
Expectation is the long-run mean: E(X) = Σ x p(x) for discrete variables, or ∫ x f(x) dx for continuous variables.

Variance measures spread: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − μ², where μ = E(X). Its square root is the standard deviation. These summaries describe the centre and spread of a distribution.

sections.heading: Common distributions
sections.text:
Common models: binomial counts successes in n independent trials with probability p; mean np, variance np(1 − p). Poisson counts events in a fixed interval with rate λ; mean and variance both λ. Normal is symmetric with mean μ and standard deviation σ; standardise with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ. Continuous uniform on [a, b] has mean (a + b) ÷ 2 and variance (b − a)² ÷ 12. Exponential models waiting time at rate λ; mean 1 ÷ λ and variance 1 ÷ λ².

Example: for Bin(10, 0.2), P(X = 3) = C(10,3)(0.2)³(0.8)⁷ = 0.2013, mean 2, variance 1.6.

keyPoints: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers; discrete variables have countable values and continuous variables have interval values.
A pmf gives P(X = x) and sums to 1; a pdf gives probability as area and integrates to 1.
The cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x) rises from 0 to 1.
E(X) = Σ x p(x) or ∫ x f(x) dx; Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
Binomial mean np and variance np(1 − p); Poisson mean and variance λ.
Normal standard score z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; uniform variance (b − a)² ÷ 12; exponential mean 1 ÷ λ.

en.title: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
en.short: Sampling variability, sampling distributions, standard error, the central limit theorem, and t, chi-square and F.

sections.heading: Sampling variability
sections.text: A statistic such as a mean or proportion changes from sample to sample, even when the population is fixed. This is sampling variability. Its probability distribution over repeated random samples is the sampling distribution of the statistic. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of that sampling distribution; it measures how much the statistic typically varies, not how much the data vary.

sections.heading: Means and proportions
sections.text:
For a random sample of size n from a population with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the sample mean Xbar has mean μ and SE = σ/√n. If the population is normal, Xbar is normal for any n. For a proportion, the sample proportion phat has mean p and SE = √(p(1−p)/n), and is approximately normal when np and n(1−p) are large enough.

Example: n = 100, σ = 10. SE = 10/√100 = 1. If μ = 50, then Xbar = 53 is z = (53 − 50)/1 = 3.

sections.heading: Variance and related distributions
sections.text: For a normal population, the sample variance S² has a sampling distribution linked to the chi-square (χ²) distribution: (n − 1)S²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom (df counts the values free to vary). When σ is unknown, the t distribution replaces the normal for the mean: t = (Xbar − μ)/(S/√n), with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The F distribution is the ratio of two independent chi-square variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom; it compares variances and appears in ANOVA (analysis of variance).

sections.heading: Central limit theorem
sections.text: The central limit theorem (CLT) says that for large n the sampling distribution of Xbar is approximately normal with mean μ and SE σ/√n, whatever the population shape, provided σ is finite. The same idea applies to sums and, under the conditions above, to proportions. 'Large' depends on the population; skewness and outliers need larger n. The CLT is why many intervals and tests use normal or t critical values.

keyPoints: A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over repeated random samples, and its standard deviation is the standard error.
For a sample mean, the mean is μ and the standard error is σ/√n; for a sample proportion, the mean is p and the standard error is √(p(1−p)/n).
The central limit theorem makes Xbar approximately normal for large n when σ is finite, whatever the population shape.
For a normal population, (n − 1)S² ÷ σ² has a chi-square distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
When σ is unknown, use t = (Xbar − μ) ÷ (S/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
The F distribution is a ratio of two independent chi-square variables, each divided by its own degrees of freedom, and it is used to compare variances.

en.title: Estimation and confidence intervals
en.short: Point estimators, method of moments, maximum likelihood, confidence intervals and sample size.

sections.heading: Point estimators
sections.text:
A point estimator is a rule for guessing an unknown population parameter from a sample; its value is an estimate. The sample mean xbar estimates μ, and the sample proportion phat estimates p.

A good estimator is unbiased (its repeated-sample average equals the parameter), efficient (small variance) and consistent (it approaches the parameter as n grows). Its standard error is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution, often estimated by s/√n.

sections.heading: Finding estimators
sections.text:
Two methods produce estimators. The method of moments equates sample moments to population moments and solves. For Bernoulli(p) data, the first moment gives phat = xbar.

Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter value that makes the observed sample most likely, by maximising the likelihood or its logarithm. For Bernoulli data the likelihood is p^r(1−p)^(n−r), where r is the number of successes; maximising gives phat = r/n. The methods often agree, but not always.

sections.heading: Intervals and sample size
sections.text:
A confidence interval is a range of plausible values, with a stated confidence level. A 95% interval comes from a method that captures the parameter in 95% of repeated samples; it is not a 95% probability for one fixed parameter. For a mean with known σ: xbar ± z σ/√n. With unknown σ, use t and s/√n. For a proportion: phat ± z√(phat(1−phat)/n). For a difference in means: (xbar1 − xbar2) ± z√(σ1²/n1 + σ2²/n2); for a difference in proportions, use phat1 − phat2 with standard error √(phat1(1−phat1)/n1 + phat2(1−phat2)/n2).

Example: n = 100, xbar = 52, σ = 10, 95% z = 1.96. Standard error = 1; margin of error = 1.96; interval 50.04 to 53.96.

The margin of error is half the width. For a target E, n = (zσ/E)², rounded up; for a proportion n = z²p(1−p)/E², using p = 0.5 if unknown.

keyPoints: A point estimator is a rule for estimating a parameter; an estimate is its calculated value.
An estimator is unbiased if its repeated-sample average equals the parameter, efficient if it has small variance, and consistent if it approaches the parameter as n grows.
Method of moments equates sample and population moments; maximum likelihood maximises the likelihood or log-likelihood.
For a mean with known σ, the confidence interval is xbar ± z σ/√n; with unknown σ use t and s/√n.
For a proportion, the interval is phat ± z√(phat(1−phat)/n); for differences use the difference with the combined standard error.
Margin of error is half the interval width; required n for a mean is (zσ/E)², rounded up, and for a proportion n = z²p(1−p)/E², using p = 0.5 if unknown.

en.title: Hypothesis testing: principles and basic tests
en.short: Null and alternative hypotheses, p-values, errors and power, and basic tests for means and proportions.

sections.heading: Hypotheses and errors
sections.text:
The null hypothesis H0 states no effect or a specified value, such as μ = 50. The alternative H1 states the suspected effect: μ ≠ 50 (two-sided), μ > 50 or μ < 50 (one-sided). We test H0, not prove it.

A Type I error rejects a true H0; its probability is the significance level α, commonly 0.05. A Type II error fails to reject a false H0; its probability is β. Power is 1 − β, the chance of detecting a real effect. Power rises with larger samples and larger effects.

sections.heading: Test statistic and p-value
sections.text:
A test statistic measures how far the estimate lies from the H0 value in standard-error units. The p-value is the probability, assuming H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed. Reject H0 if p < α. A small p-value is evidence against H0, not the probability H0 is true.

Example: test H0: μ = 50 against H1: μ ≠ 50 with n = 36, x̄ = 53, σ = 9. Then z = (53 − 50) ÷ (9 ÷ √36) = 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2.00. For a two-sided test at α = 0.05, the critical values are ±1.96. Since 2.00 > 1.96, reject H0. The two-sided p-value is about 0.046.

sections.heading: Means and proportions
sections.text:
For one mean, use z = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) if σ is known; use t = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (s ÷ √n) if σ is unknown, with n − 1 degrees of freedom. For two independent means, use the difference divided by its standard error, √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2).

For one proportion, z = (p̂ − p0) ÷ √(p0(1 − p0) ÷ n). For two proportions, pool the estimates: p̂ = (x1 + x2) ÷ (n1 + n2), then z = (p̂1 − p̂2) ÷ √(p̂(1 − p̂)(1/n1 + 1/n2)). Assume random, independent samples with enough successes and failures.

keyPoints: H0 states no effect or a specified value; H1 states the alternative, and we test H0 rather than prove it.
A Type I error rejects a true H0 with probability α; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0 with probability β; power is 1 − β.
The p-value is the probability, assuming H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed; reject H0 when p < α.
One-sample mean test: z = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) when σ is known, or t = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (s ÷ √n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
Two-sample mean test: z or t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2).
One-proportion test: z = (p̂ − p0) ÷ √(p0(1 − p0) ÷ n); two-proportion test pools p̂ = (x1 + x2) ÷ (n1 + n2).

en.title: Correlation and simple linear regression
en.short: Scatterplots and correlation, the least squares line, residuals, R squared, and testing the slope.

sections.heading: Scatterplots and correlation
sections.text:
A scatterplot puts one variable on each axis, one point per case. Look for direction, strength, curvature and outliers first.

The correlation coefficient is r = Sxy ÷ √(Sxx × Syy), where Sxx = Σ(x − x̄)², Syy = Σ(y − ȳ)² and Sxy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ). It runs from −1 to +1 and measures only straight-line association. Swapping the axes or changing units leaves it unchanged.

It is not resistant: one outlier can move it a long way. And r = 0 means no linear relationship, not no relationship.

sections.heading: Least squares line
sections.text:
The line ŷ = a + bx is fitted by least squares: choose a and b so the sum of squared residuals is as small as possible. The solution is b = Sxy ÷ Sxx and a = ȳ − b x̄, so the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

Example: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. Then x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4, Sxx = 10 and Sxy = 6.
b = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6
a = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2
So ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x.

sections.heading: Residuals and R squared
sections.text:
A residual is e = y − ŷ, the vertical gap between a point and the line. With an intercept fitted, residuals sum to zero, and a residual plot should show no pattern.

R² = 1 − SSE ÷ Syy is the share of variation in y explained by the line. Here the fitted values are 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2, so SSE = 0.64 + 0.36 + 1.00 + 0.36 + 0.04 = 2.40. With Syy = 6, R² = 1 − 2.40 ÷ 6 = 0.60.

sections.heading: Inference and caution
sections.text:
The slope is a sample estimate. Its standard error is SE(b) = s ÷ √Sxx, where s² = SSE ÷ (n − 2). A test of β = 0 uses t = b ÷ SE(b) with n − 2 degrees of freedom. Here s² = 2.40 ÷ 3 = 0.8, so SE(b) = 0.894 ÷ √10 = 0.283 and t = 0.6 ÷ 0.283 = 2.12 on 3 df.

Correlation is not causation: a strong r may reflect a lurking variable, or y may cause x. Random assignment in an experiment supports a causal claim; random sampling helps results generalise, but observational data alone usually cannot establish causation.

keyPoints: Correlation r = Sxy ÷ √(Sxx × Syy) measures straight-line association only, from −1 to +1.
Least squares gives b = Sxy ÷ Sxx and a = ȳ − b x̄, so the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
A residual is y − ŷ; residuals sum to zero and should show no pattern in a plot.
R² = 1 − SSE ÷ Syy is the share of variation in y explained by the line.
SE(b) = s ÷ √Sxx with s² = SSE ÷ (n − 2), and t = b ÷ SE(b) on n − 2 df.
A strong correlation does not by itself show that x causes y.

en.title: Categorical data: contingency tables and chi-square tests
en.short: Contingency tables, marginal and conditional distributions, chi-square tests, odds and risk ratios.

sections.heading: Tables and distributions
sections.text:
A contingency table cross-tabulates two categorical variables: rows are levels of one, columns levels of the other, cells hold counts. Marginal distributions are row and column totals as proportions of the grand total.

A conditional distribution fixes one variable and gives proportions across the other. The variables are independent when every conditional distribution is the same at each level of the other. Then expected count E = row total × column total ÷ grand total.

sections.heading: Chi-square tests
sections.text:
The chi-square test of independence tests whether two categorical variables are associated. The null hypothesis is independence. Compute X² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E over cells, with E as above. Degrees of freedom are (r − 1)(c − 1). A large X² gives a small p-value, evidence against independence.

Example: 100 exposed and 100 unexposed people. Outcome yes: 30 exposed, 20 unexposed; no: 70 and 80. Column totals are 50 yes, 150 no. Expected yes counts are 100 × 50 ÷ 200 = 25; expected no counts are 75. X² = (30−25)²/25 + (70−75)²/75 + (20−25)²/25 + (80−75)²/75 = 2.667. With df = 1 this is below 3.841, the 5% critical value, so there is no significant evidence of association.

A goodness-of-fit test compares one variable with stated proportions. Expected counts are E = n p; df = k − 1 for k categories, fewer if proportions were estimated. Use the same X² formula.

sections.heading: Odds and risk ratios
sections.text:
For a 2×2 table, risk is the proportion with the outcome in a group. Here risk is 30 ÷ 100 = 0.30 exposed and 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20 unexposed, so risk ratio = 0.30 ÷ 0.20 = 1.5.

Odds are cases ÷ non-cases: 30 ÷ 70 = 0.429 and 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25, so odds ratio = 0.429 ÷ 0.25 = 1.714, also ad ÷ bc. The ratios differ; they are close only when the outcome is rare. Association is not proof of causation.

keyPoints: A contingency table cross-tabulates counts of two categorical variables.
Marginal distributions use row or column totals; conditional distributions fix one variable.
Under independence, expected counts are E = row total × column total ÷ grand total for every cell.
Chi-square statistic: X² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E; independence df = (r − 1)(c − 1).
Goodness of fit uses E = n p and df = k − 1 minus any estimated parameters.
Risk ratio = risk1 ÷ risk2; odds ratio = (a ÷ b) ÷ (c ÷ d) = ad ÷ bc.

en.title: Multiple linear regression
en.short: Covers matrix least squares, coefficient inference, residual checks, collinearity, interactions and variable selection.

sections.heading: Matrix model
sections.text: Model: y = Xβ + ε. y is the n × 1 response, X the n × p design matrix with first column ones, β the p × 1 coefficients, and ε independent errors with mean 0 and variance σ², so ε ~ (0, σ²I). Each row of X is one observation. βj is the expected change in y per one-unit rise in xj, other predictors fixed.

sections.heading: Least squares
sections.text: Least squares minimises SSE = (y − Xβ)ᵀ(y − Xβ). The normal equations are XᵀXβhat = Xᵀy, so βhat = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when XᵀX is invertible. Fitted values are yhat = Xβhat; residuals e = y − yhat. Estimate σ² by σhat² = eᵀe ÷ (n − p), p counting the intercept. Example: n = 4, p = 3, x1 = (−1,−1,1,1), x2 = (−1,1,−1,1), y = (2,4,6,9). Then XᵀX = 4I, Xᵀy = (21,9,5), βhat = (5.25,2.25,1.25). Residuals are (0.25,−0.25,−0.25,0.25), SSE = 0.25, σhat² = 0.25.

sections.heading: Inference
sections.text: βhat is unbiased with Var(βhat) = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹. The standard error of βjhat is the square root of the jth diagonal entry of σhat²(XᵀX)⁻¹. With normal errors, a 95% interval is βjhat ± t SE, with t the 0.975 quantile of t on n − p degrees of freedom. Test H0: βj = 0 by t = βjhat ÷ SE. In the example each SE = √(0.25 × 1/4) = 0.25; df = 1 makes intervals very wide.

sections.heading: Diagnostics and selection
sections.text: Plot residuals against fitted values and on a normal Q-Q plot; check curvature, changing spread, outliers and influential points (leverage, Cook’s distance). Multicollinearity means predictors are correlated. VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − Rj²), where Rj² is from regressing xj on the others; large VIF inflates standard errors. An interaction x1x2 lets the effect of x1 depend on x2. Select variables using subject knowledge, adjusted R², AIC or BIC, and cross-validation; stepwise selection can overfit.

keyPoints: Model: y = Xβ + ε, with ε ~ (0, σ²I); X has a first column of ones.
Least squares: βhat = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy and σhat² = eᵀe ÷ (n − p).
Var(βhat) = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹; a coefficient interval is βjhat ± t SE with n − p degrees of freedom.
Check residuals for curvature, unequal variance, outliers and influential points before trusting inference.
VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − Rj²) measures multicollinearity; large values inflate standard errors.
An interaction x1x2 means the effect of x1 changes with x2; choose variables with knowledge, AIC/BIC or cross-validation, not stepwise alone.

en.title: Analysis of variance
en.short: One-way and two-way ANOVA, fixed effects, assumptions, diagnostics, contrasts and post-hoc tests.

sections.heading: One-way ANOVA
sections.text:
One-way ANOVA compares the means of k independent groups. The fixed effects model is y_ij = μ + τ_i + ε_ij, where μ is the overall mean, τ_i is the group effect (Στ_i = 0) and ε_ij are independent N(0, σ²) errors. It tests H0: all τ_i = 0.

The variation splits: SST = SSB + SSW. With N observations and k groups, F = [SSB/(k−1)] ÷ [SSW/(N−k)]. A large F means between-group variation is large relative to within-group variation.

Example: groups A 4,6,5,5; B 7,9,8,8; C 10,12,11,11. Means 5,8,11; grand mean 8. SSB = 4[(5−8)²+(8−8)²+(11−8)²] = 72, df 2. SSW = 6, df 9. F = (72/2) ÷ (6/9) = 36 ÷ 0.667 = 54.

sections.heading: Two-way ANOVA
sections.text: Two-way ANOVA studies two factors at once, such as fertiliser and irrigation. The balanced fixed effects model is y_ijk = μ + α_i + β_j + (αβ)_ij + ε_ijk. The interaction (αβ)_ij lets the effect of one factor depend on the level of the other. Total variation splits into SS_A, SS_B, SS_AB and SS_error. Each effect is tested by F = MS_effect ÷ MS_error. If interaction is significant, interpret main effects with care.

sections.heading: Assumptions and diagnostics
sections.text: ANOVA assumes independent observations, normal errors and equal error variances. Check residuals, not raw data: plot residuals against fitted values, and use a normal Q-Q plot. Levene’s test checks equal variances; Bartlett’s test is sensitive to non-normality. Outliers, unequal group sizes and transformations (log, square root) matter. Randomisation supports independence.

sections.heading: Contrasts and post-hoc
sections.text: A contrast is L = Σc_i ȳ_i with Σc_i = 0. It answers a planned question, such as group 1 versus groups 2 and 3. Test it with t = L ÷ SE(L), where SE(L) = √[MSW Σ(c_i²/n_i)]. Post-hoc comparisons (Tukey, Scheffé, Bonferroni) control familywise error after a significant F test. Tukey suits all pairwise comparisons; Scheffé is flexible for any contrast but wider.

keyPoints: One-way ANOVA splits SST = SSB + SSW and tests F = [SSB/(k−1)] ÷ [SSW/(N−k)].
The fixed effects model is y_ij = μ + τ_i + ε_ij with independent N(0, σ²) errors.
Two-way ANOVA includes two main effects and an interaction term (αβ)_ij.
ANOVA assumes independence, normal errors and equal variances; check residuals and use Levene’s test.
A contrast L = Σc_i ȳ_i with Σc_i = 0 is tested by t = L ÷ SE(L).
Post-hoc tests such as Tukey and Scheffé control familywise error after a significant F test.

en.title: Design of experiments
en.short: Randomisation, blocking, factorial and fractional designs, split-plot and repeated measures, power and sample size.

sections.heading: Principles and blocking
sections.text: Randomisation assigns treatments to units by chance, protecting against hidden bias and supporting valid inference. Replication repeats treatments on independent units, giving an estimate of experimental error and increasing precision. Blocking groups similar units, such as plots in one field, and randomises treatments within each block. Good blocking removes a known source of variation from the error.

sections.heading: Factorial designs
sections.text: A factorial design tests all combinations of the levels of two or more factors. In a 2² design, two factors each have two levels, giving four treatment combinations. Each observation helps estimate main effects and interactions. An interaction means the effect of one factor changes with the level of another. A fractional factorial design uses a chosen subset of combinations when the full design would need too many runs, for example with many factors. It saves runs but aliases effects, so some cannot be separated. Resolution states what is aliased.

sections.heading: Split-plot and repeated measures
sections.text: A split-plot design is used when one factor is hard to change. Whole plots, groups of subplots, are randomised to its levels, and subplots within each whole plot are randomised to the other factor. It has two error terms, one for whole plots and one for subplots, so analysis differs from a fully randomised factorial. Repeated measures arise when the same unit is measured several times, such as a patient at weeks 1, 4 and 8. The measurements are correlated, so use a model that allows correlation, such as a mixed-effects model.

sections.heading: Power and sample size
sections.text: Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a real effect exists. It rises with larger effects, lower variability, larger samples and higher α. For two equal groups comparing means, an approximate sample size per group is n = 2(z(1−α/2) + z(1−β))² σ² ÷ Δ², where Δ is the difference worth detecting and σ the standard deviation. Example: σ = 10, Δ = 5, α = 0.05 two-sided, power = 0.80. Then n = 2(1.96 + 0.84)² × 100 ÷ 25 = 62.72, so 63 per group. Check assumptions and use software for exact designs.

keyPoints: Randomisation, replication and blocking protect against bias and reduce experimental error.
In a 2² factorial there are four treatment combinations; interactions show that one factor’s effect depends on another.
Fractional factorials save runs but alias some effects; resolution describes the aliasing.
Split-plot designs have whole-plot and subplot error terms; repeated measures need a correlation model.
Power is the probability of detecting a real effect, and it increases with effect size, sample size and α.
For two equal groups comparing means, n per group ≈ 2(z(1−α/2) + z(1−β))² σ² ÷ Δ².

en.title: Categorical data analysis: logistic and log-linear models
en.short: Binary and multinomial logistic regression, odds ratios, log-linear models, deviance and fit.

sections.heading: Binary logistic model
sections.text:
Binary logistic regression models p = P(Y = 1) by logit(p) = ln(p ÷ (1 − p)) = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk. The inverse is p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−η). βj is the change in log odds per unit xj, other predictors fixed. The odds ratio is OR = e^βj. OR = 1 means no effect; OR = 2 doubles odds, not probability. For a categorical predictor, e^β compares its level with the reference level.

Example: β1 = 0.693 gives OR = e^0.693 = 2.00. If p = 0.20, odds = 0.25. Doubled odds = 0.50, so p = 0.50 ÷ 1.50 = 0.333.

sections.heading: Multinomial and deviance
sections.text:
Multinomial logistic regression handles a nominal outcome with J > 2 categories. With category J as baseline, ln(P(Y = j) ÷ P(Y = J)) = βj0 + βj1x. Then e^βj1 is the relative odds ratio for j against J per unit x. Fit by maximum likelihood.

Deviance is D = −2(ln Lmodel − ln Lsaturated), where the saturated model fits the data exactly. For nested models, ΔD = D(reduced) − D(full) is approximately chi-square with df equal to extra parameters. Large ΔD supports the extra terms. Small deviance relative to df suggests adequate fit, but check df and purpose.

sections.heading: Log-linear models
sections.text:
Log-linear models describe counts in a contingency table as a Poisson regression with log link: ln μij = λ + λi^A + λj^B + λij^AB. Main effects and interactions are λ terms. The independence model omits λij^AB; the saturated model includes all terms and fits exactly. An interaction shows association.

Goodness of fit uses G² = 2 Σ O ln(O ÷ E), with O observed and E expected. df = cells − fitted parameters. Compare G² with chi-square. In a 2×2 table the independence model has 4 cells and 3 parameters, so df = 1. If G² = 3.84, p about 0.05.

keyPoints: Binary logistic regression: logit(p) = ln(p ÷ (1 − p)) = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk.
The odds ratio for a one unit change in xj is OR = e^βj; OR = 2 doubles odds, not probability.
Multinomial logistic compares each category j with baseline J: ln(P(Y = j) ÷ P(Y = J)) = βj0 + βj1x, and e^βj1 is a relative odds ratio.
A log-linear model is a Poisson regression for counts: ln μ = λ + main effects + interactions; independence means no interaction.
Deviance D = −2(ln Lmodel − ln Lsaturated); nested models are compared by ΔD, approximately chi-square with df equal to the difference in parameters.
For log-linear fit, G² = 2ΣO ln(O ÷ E) with df = cells − parameters; a large G² against chi-square indicates poor fit.

en.title: Nonparametric statistics
en.short: Rank, sign and permutation tests for when distributional assumptions are doubtful.

sections.heading: Signs and signed ranks
sections.text:
Nonparametric methods use ranks or signs, not an assumed distribution. The sign test counts positive paired differences. Under the null of no systematic difference, each sign is equally likely, so the count is Binomial(n, 0.5). It ignores sizes. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks absolute differences and compares the sum of positive ranks, W+. Ties get average ranks; zero differences are dropped.

Example: differences 2, −1, 4, 5, −3, 6, 1, −2. Their absolute values 2, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 2 get ranks 3.5, 1.5, 6, 7, 5, 8, 1.5, 3.5. Then W+ = 3.5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 1.5 = 26 and W− = 1.5 + 5 + 3.5 = 10. Tables or a normal approximation give the p-value.

sections.heading: Two or more groups
sections.text: Mann-Whitney U compares two independent samples. Pool and rank all observations; U counts how often a value from one group precedes one from the other. Under the null, group labels are randomly mixed. Kruskal-Wallis extends this to three or more groups: rank all observations and compare group mean ranks. Its statistic H is approximately chi-square with k − 1 degrees of freedom for moderate group sizes.

sections.heading: Rank correlation
sections.text:
Spearman’s rho is the Pearson correlation of the ranks. With no ties, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)), where d is the difference in ranks for each pair. Kendall’s tau counts concordant and discordant pairs. Both lie between −1 and 1.

Example: five pairs have rank differences −1, 1, −1, 1, 0, so Σd² = 4. Then rs = 1 − 6×4 ÷ (5×24) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.

sections.heading: Permutation tests
sections.text: A permutation test builds the null distribution by repeatedly shuffling labels or signs. It assumes exchangeability under the null hypothesis, not normality. The p-value is the proportion of shuffled statistics at least as extreme as the observed one. Enumerating all permutations gives an exact test; random permutations give a Monte Carlo approximation. They suit doubtful distributional assumptions but cannot repair biased sampling or confounding.

keyPoints: Sign test: the number of positive paired differences is Binomial(n, 0.5) under the null hypothesis.
Wilcoxon signed-rank: rank absolute differences and use W+ = sum of ranks of positive differences.
Mann-Whitney U = R1 − n1(n1 + 1) ÷ 2, where R1 is the rank sum of group 1.
Kruskal-Wallis H = [12 ÷ (N(N + 1))] Σ n_i Rbar_i² − 3(N + 1), with k − 1 degrees of freedom.
Spearman’s rho with no ties: rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).
A permutation p-value is the proportion of permuted statistics at least as extreme as the observed statistic.

en.title: Multivariate analysis
en.short: Multivariate normal, Hotelling T², principal components, factor, discriminant and cluster analysis.

sections.heading: Normal and Hotelling
sections.text:
A random vector x is multivariate normal if every linear combination of its components is normal. It is described by a mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ. Its density depends on the squared Mahalanobis distance (x−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μ). Marginals and conditionals are normal, and zero covariance means independence.

Hotelling’s T² tests a mean vector. For one sample, T² = n(x̄−μ₀)ᵀS⁻¹(x̄−μ₀), and [(n−p)/(p(n−1))]T² ~ F(p, n−p) under the null. For two samples, use x̄₁−x̄₂, pooled S, and factor n₁n₂/(n₁+n₂).

Example: n = 10, p = 2, x̄ = (1,2), S = [[2,1],[1,3]], μ₀ = (0,0). S⁻¹ = (1/5)[[3,−1],[−1,2]], so x̄ᵀS⁻¹x̄ = 7/5 and T² = 14. Then F = (8/18)×14 = 6.22. The 5% critical value F(2,8) = 4.46, so reject μ₀.

sections.heading: Components and factors
sections.text: Principal component analysis (PCA) finds linear combinations of the variables with maximum variance. The first component has variance equal to the largest eigenvalue of the covariance or correlation matrix, and its weights are the matching eigenvector. Standardise variables when units differ. Factor analysis models each variable as a linear function of a few unobserved common factors plus a unique error: x = μ + Λf + ε. It seeks latent factors that explain the correlations. PCA is a variance-reduction technique; factor analysis is a latent-variable model, and its factors are often rotated for interpretation.

sections.heading: Discriminant and cluster
sections.text: Discriminant analysis classifies observations into known groups. Fisher’s linear discriminant finds the direction that best separates group means. Linear discriminant analysis assumes each group is multivariate normal with the same covariance matrix; quadratic discriminant analysis allows different covariances. Cluster analysis finds groups when labels are unknown. K-means partitions points into k clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squared distances. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested groups. Distances such as Euclidean distance measure dissimilarity; smaller distance means more similar. Always standardise variables before clustering if their scales differ.

keyPoints: The multivariate normal density is f(x) = (2π)^(−p/2)|Σ|^(−1/2) exp[−½(x−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μ)].
Hotelling’s one-sample T² = n(x̄−μ₀)ᵀS⁻¹(x̄−μ₀), and [(n−p)/(p(n−1))]T² ~ F(p, n−p).
For two samples, T² uses x̄₁−x̄₂, pooled S and factor n₁n₂/(n₁+n₂).
In PCA, each component’s variance is its eigenvalue; standardise when units differ.
Factor analysis models x = μ + Λf + ε, with common factors f and unique errors ε.
LDA assumes equal covariance matrices across groups; k-means minimises within-cluster squared distances.

en.title: Time series analysis: trend, seasonality and ARIMA
en.short: Trend, seasonality, stationarity, ACF/PACF, ARIMA models, forecasting and diagnostics.

sections.heading: Trend and seasonality
sections.text: A time series is a sequence of observations ordered in time, such as monthly sales. Trend is the slow long-run movement. Seasonality repeats at a fixed period, for example every 12 months. Plot the series first. A moving average can estimate trend; seasonal indices estimate repeating effects. Do not confuse seasonality with a cycle, whose period is not fixed.

sections.heading: Stationarity and correlations
sections.text: Weak stationarity means the mean, variance and autocovariance do not change with time. Many ARIMA methods assume it. A stationary series tends to return to its mean. The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures correlation between y_t and y_{t−k}. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures their correlation after removing the effects of shorter lags. For a stationary AR(1) model y_t = μ + φ(y_{t−1} − μ) + ε_t, the ACF at lag k is ρ_k = φ^k, and stationarity requires |φ| < 1.

sections.heading: ARIMA models
sections.text: ARIMA(p,d,q) combines autoregression (AR), differencing (d) and moving average (MA) errors. Differencing d times removes trend and makes the series roughly stationary. Write φ(B)(1−B)^d y_t = θ(B)ε_t, where B is the backshift operator, so B y_t = y_{t−1}. Seasonal ARIMA adds seasonal terms: (p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_m, with m the seasonal period. Use ACF and PACF as guides: an AR(p) has PACF cutting off after lag p; an MA(q) has ACF cutting off after lag q. In practice compare candidate models by Akaike’s information criterion (AIC) and check residuals.

sections.heading: Forecasting and diagnostics
sections.text: Forecasting uses the fitted model. For a stationary AR(1) with mean μ = 100, φ = 0.6 and last value y_T = 120, the one-step forecast is 100 + 0.6(120 − 100) = 112. The two-step forecast is 100 + 0.6(112 − 100) = 107.2. Forecast error grows with horizon. Diagnostics check that residuals look like white noise: zero mean, constant variance, no correlation. Plot them, inspect residual ACF, and use the Ljung-Box test. Refit if large spikes or test evidence remain.

keyPoints: A time series has trend, seasonality and irregular variation; plot it before modelling.
Weak stationarity means constant mean, variance and autocovariance; AR(1) needs |φ| < 1 and has ACF ρ_k = φ^k.
ACF and PACF help identify AR and MA orders, but model choice should use AIC and residual checks.
ARIMA(p,d,q) is φ(B)(1−B)^d y_t = θ(B)ε_t; seasonal ARIMA adds (P,D,Q)_m terms.
For a stationary AR(1), forecast ŷ_{T+h} = μ + φ^h(y_T − μ).
Check residuals with plots, residual ACF and the Ljung-Box test; refit if they are not white noise.

en.title: Survey sampling methods
en.short: Frames, simple random, stratified, cluster and multistage sampling, weights, nonresponse and design effects.

sections.heading: Frames and SRS
sections.text:
A sampling frame is a list or map of population units. It should cover the target population once, with no gaps or duplicates. Undercoverage biases estimates because some units can never be selected.

Simple random sampling (SRS) gives every sample of size n the same chance. Use random numbers. For sample values y_i, the mean estimate is ybar = Σy_i/n and the total estimate is T = N ybar. The variance of ybar is about (1 − n/N)s²/n; (1 − n/N) is the finite population correction.

sections.heading: Stratified, cluster, multistage
sections.text:
Stratified sampling splits the frame into strata, such as states or age groups, and samples independently inside each. Proportional allocation sets n_h = n N_h/N. Neyman allocation, proportional to N_h s_h, is often efficient. Stratification helps when units within a stratum are alike.

Cluster sampling selects whole clusters, such as villages or schools, and studies units inside. It is cheaper but usually less precise because units in a cluster are similar. Multistage sampling combines stages: select clusters, then households, then people.

sections.heading: Weights and nonresponse
sections.text:
Each unit has inclusion probability π_i, so base weight w_i = 1/π_i. Weighted total = Σw_i y_i; weighted mean = Σw_i y_i ÷ Σw_i. Weights correct unequal selection and can be adjusted for nonresponse within classes. Report response rates and weight adjustments.

Design effect deff = design variance ÷ SRS variance at same n. Cluster designs often have deff > 1; good stratification can give deff < 1. Effective sample size ≈ n ÷ deff.

sections.heading: Design effects and example
sections.text: Example: N = 5 values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. SRS n = 2 gives 20 and 40. Mean estimate = (20 + 40) ÷ 2 = 30; total estimate = 5 × 30 = 150. s² = ((20 − 30)² + (40 − 30)²) ÷ (2 − 1) = 200. Estimated variance of mean = (1 − 2/5) × 200 ÷ 2 = 60, so standard error = √60 = 7.75. Total standard error = 5 × 7.75 = 38.7.

keyPoints: A sampling frame must cover the target population once, without gaps or duplicates.
In SRS, ybar = Σy_i/n estimates the mean and T = N ybar estimates the total, with variance about (1 − n/N)s²/n.
Stratified sampling samples within strata and can reduce variance; cluster sampling selects whole clusters and often increases it.
Base weight w_i = 1/π_i; weighted total = Σw_i y_i and weighted mean = Σw_i y_i ÷ Σw_i.
Nonresponse is handled by adjusting weights within response classes and reporting response rates.
Design effect deff = design variance ÷ SRS variance; effective sample size is about n ÷ deff.

en.title: Statistical quality control: charts, capability and sampling
en.short: Shewhart, CUSUM and EWMA charts, process capability and acceptance sampling.

sections.heading: Shewhart charts
sections.text:
A control chart plots a sample statistic over time with a centre line and control limits. Shewhart Xbar limits are μ ± 3σ/√n when μ and σ are known; an R or s chart tracks within-sample variation.

Limits come from the process, not from specifications. A point outside a limit, or a run or trend, suggests a special cause.

sections.heading: CUSUM and EWMA
sections.text:
CUSUM adds deviations from target: C⁺_i = max(0, C⁺_(i−1) + (x_i − μ0) − k) and C⁻_i = max(0, C⁻_(i−1) − (x_i − μ0) − k). Here k is a reference value and h a decision interval; a signal occurs when either exceeds h.

EWMA smooths: Z_i = λx_i + (1 − λ)Z_(i−1), with asymptotic limits μ0 ± Lσ√(λ ÷ (2 − λ)). λ is a smoothing constant between 0 and 1; L sets the limit width. Small λ and CUSUM detect small persistent shifts; Shewhart charts suit larger shifts.

sections.heading: Process capability
sections.text:
Capability compares process spread with specification limits. Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ), where USL and LSL are the upper and lower specification limits. Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ (3σ).

Example: USL = 56, LSL = 44, μ = 50, σ = 2. Cp = 12 ÷ 12 = 1.00. Cpk = min(6, 6) ÷ 6 = 1.00. If μ = 51, Cpk = min(5, 7) ÷ 6 = 0.83. A capable process is stable first; capability indices assume normality and a controlled process.

sections.heading: Acceptance sampling
sections.text:
Acceptance sampling decides whether to accept a lot from a sample, using a plan (n, c): accept if the number of defective items is at most c. The OC (operating characteristic) curve gives the probability of acceptance for each lot quality.

Producer’s risk α is rejecting a good lot; consumer’s risk β is accepting a bad lot. AQL (acceptable quality level) and LTPD (lot tolerance percent defective) are agreed quality levels. On any chart, investigate a signal for an assignable cause before adjusting the process.

keyPoints: Control limits come from the process; specification limits come from requirements.
Shewhart Xbar limits are μ ± 3σ/√n; R or s charts monitor variation.
CUSUM signals when C⁺_i or C⁻_i exceeds h.
EWMA is Z_i = λx_i + (1 − λ)Z_(i−1); small λ detects small shifts.
Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ) and Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ (3σ).
Acceptance sampling uses an OC curve; α is producer’s risk and β is consumer’s risk.

en.title: Stochastic processes: Markov chains, Poisson processes and queues
en.short: Markov chains, Poisson processes, birth-death and queuing models, and reliability and service applications.

sections.heading: Markov chains
sections.text:
A Markov chain is a sequence of states where the next state depends only on the present state. The transition probability p_ij is the chance of moving from i to j. The transition matrix P has rows summing to 1, and P^n gives n-step probabilities.

A stationary distribution π satisfies π = πP and sums to 1. Example: P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]]. From π1 = 0.9π1 + 0.2π2 and π1 + π2 = 1, we get π1 = 2π2, so π = (2/3, 1/3).

sections.heading: Poisson process
sections.text:
A Poisson process counts events occurring randomly in time at rate λ. The count N(t) by time t is Poisson with mean λt: P(N(t) = k) = e^(−λt)(λt)^k ÷ k!. Counts in disjoint intervals are independent.

Interarrival times are exponential with mean 1/λ. If λ = 3 per hour, the chance of no event in 10 minutes is e^(−3 × 1/6) = e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.607.

sections.heading: Birth-death and queues
sections.text:
A birth-death process moves up by one at rate λ_n and down by one at rate μ_n. The M/M/1 queue has Poisson arrivals at rate λ, exponential service at rate μ, one server, and ρ = λ ÷ μ < 1.

Its steady-state probability of n customers is p_n = (1 − ρ)ρ^n. The mean number is L = ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) = λ ÷ (μ − λ), and Little’s law gives mean time W = 1 ÷ (μ − λ).

Example: λ = 4 per hour, μ = 5 per hour. Then ρ = 0.8, L = 4, W = 1 hour.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.text:
In reliability, a repairable component is a two-state Markov chain: working and failed. With failure rate λ and repair rate μ, steady-state availability is A = μ ÷ (λ + μ). Poisson processes model random failures at constant rate.

In service systems, queuing models estimate waiting times and staffing needs in call centres, clinics and banks. As ρ approaches 1, congestion rises sharply.

keyPoints: A Markov chain’s next state depends only on the present state; its transition matrix P has rows summing to 1 and P^n gives n-step probabilities.
A stationary distribution satisfies π = πP and sums to 1; for P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]] it is (2/3, 1/3).
In a Poisson process with rate λ, N(t) is Poisson with mean λt and interarrival times are exponential with mean 1/λ.
In an M/M/1 queue with ρ = λ ÷ μ < 1, p_n = (1 − ρ)ρ^n, L = ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) = λ ÷ (μ − λ), and W = 1 ÷ (μ − λ).
A birth-death process moves up at rate λ_n and down at rate μ_n; many queues are birth-death processes.
For a repairable component with failure rate λ and repair rate μ, steady-state availability is A = μ ÷ (λ + μ).

en.title: Bayesian inference
en.short: Priors and posteriors, conjugate models, credible intervals, prediction, Bayes factors and an introduction to MCMC.

sections.heading: Prior and posterior
sections.text: Bayesian inference treats an unknown parameter θ as a random variable with a prior distribution, which expresses belief before data. The likelihood is the probability of the data given θ. Bayes’ theorem gives posterior ∝ prior × likelihood. The posterior expresses belief after data. Its mean, median or mode can be a point estimate, and the full distribution describes uncertainty. The prior matters with little data, so justify it and check sensitivity.

sections.heading: Conjugate models
sections.text: A conjugate prior yields a posterior in the same family, so updating is simple algebra. The Beta distribution is conjugate for Bernoulli and binomial likelihoods. If θ has prior Beta(a, b) and we observe x successes in n trials, the posterior is Beta(a + x, b + n − x). Its mean is (a + x) ÷ (a + b + n). Example: prior Beta(2, 2), then 7 successes in 10 trials. Posterior Beta(9, 5), mean 9 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.643; prior mean 0.5.

sections.heading: Intervals and Bayes factors
sections.text: A 95% credible interval contains θ with posterior probability 0.95. It is not a confidence interval. The posterior predictive distribution predicts a new observation by averaging the likelihood over the posterior. In the Beta example, the next trial is a success with probability 9 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.643. A Bayes factor compares models: BF10 = p(data | M1) ÷ p(data | M0). Values near 1 give little evidence; larger values favour M1. Labelling conventions vary, so report the number and priors.

sections.heading: Markov chain Monte Carlo
sections.text: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws dependent samples from a Markov chain whose long-run distribution is the posterior. Metropolis-Hastings proposes a move and accepts it with a probability based on the posterior ratio. Gibbs sampling updates one parameter at a time from its full conditional distribution. Use MCMC when conjugacy fails or the posterior is high-dimensional. Check convergence with several chains and diagnostics.

keyPoints: Bayes’ theorem: posterior ∝ prior × likelihood.
For Beta(a, b) prior and x successes in n Bernoulli trials, posterior is Beta(a + x, b + n − x).
Posterior mean in that model is (a + x) ÷ (a + b + n); with Beta(2, 2) and 7 of 10 it is 9 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.643.
A 95% credible interval has posterior probability 0.95 and is not a confidence interval.
Bayes factor BF10 = p(data | M1) ÷ p(data | M0) compares two models.
MCMC, including Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling, approximates posteriors when conjugacy fails; check convergence.

en.title: Statistical computing and simulation
en.short: Programming, random number generation, Monte Carlo, numerical optimisation and reproducible workflows.

sections.heading: Programming for data
sections.text: R and Python are the common languages. R is built for statistics and graphics; Python is general purpose and strong for machine learning. In both, work with vectors and data frames rather than one number at a time. A script records every step, so the analysis can be rerun. Learn to read data, clean it, fit a model and plot results. Keep code simple and check small examples by hand.

sections.heading: Random numbers and simulation
sections.text: Computers produce pseudo-random numbers from a deterministic algorithm. A seed sets the starting state, so the same seed and code give the same stream. This makes examples repeatable, but the numbers are not truly random. Simulation draws samples from a model to study its behaviour. For example, simulate 1,000 samples of size 30 from a normal distribution, compute the mean each time, and inspect the spread. This shows sampling variation without a formula.

sections.heading: Monte Carlo methods
sections.text: Monte Carlo methods estimate a quantity by repeated random sampling. Draw many points in the unit square. The proportion inside the quarter circle x² + y² ≤ 1 estimates π ÷ 4. If 7,854 of 10,000 points fall inside, the estimate is 4 × 0.7854 = 3.1416. The standard error of the proportion is √(p(1 − p) ÷ n) = √(0.7854 × 0.2146 ÷ 10,000) ≈ 0.0041, so the estimate of π has standard error about 0.0164. More draws reduce error, but only as 1 ÷ √n.

sections.heading: Optimisation and reproducibility
sections.text: Numerical optimisation finds the input that makes a function largest or smallest. Newton-Raphson uses derivatives; gradient descent steps downhill. In R use optim(); in Python use scipy.optimize. Check convergence and try several starting values. A reproducible workflow keeps scripts, raw data, seeds and package versions together, under version control such as Git. Record sessionInfo() in R or pip freeze in Python. Then another person can rerun the analysis and get the same numbers.

keyPoints: Use R or Python scripts so every step can be rerun.
Set a seed before random draws to make simulation results repeatable.
Monte Carlo estimates a quantity by repeated random sampling; error falls as 1 ÷ √n.
In the quarter-circle example, p estimates π ÷ 4, so π ≈ 4p, with standard error √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).
Numerical optimisation searches for a maximum or minimum; check convergence and try several starting values.
Reproducible workflows record code, data, seeds and package versions.

en.title: Survival analysis: time-to-event data
en.short: Censoring, survival and hazard functions, Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Cox model and checks.

sections.heading: Censoring and functions
sections.text:
Survival analysis studies time until an event, such as death, relapse or failure. Right censoring means the event was not seen before follow-up ended; we know only that the time exceeds the censoring time. The survival function S(t) = P(T > t) is the probability of surviving beyond t.

The hazard h(t) is the immediate event rate among those still at risk: h(t) = lim Δt→0 P(t ≤ T < t+Δt | T ≥ t) ÷ Δt. The cumulative hazard H(t) = ∫₀ᵗ h(u) du, and S(t) = exp(−H(t)).

sections.heading: Kaplan-Meier and log-rank
sections.text:
The Kaplan-Meier estimator is S_hat(t) = ∏_{t_i ≤ t}(1 − d_i ÷ n_i), where d_i events occur at time t_i among n_i still at risk. Censored times reduce n_i but do not count as events. The log-rank test compares two or more survival curves; under the null hypothesis of equal survival, its statistic is approximately chi-square.

Example: times 2, 4, 4, 7(censored), 9, all events except 7. At t=2, S=1−1/5=0.8. At t=4, S=0.8×(1−2/4)=0.4. At t=9, S=0.4×(1−1/1)=0. Median survival is 4.

sections.heading: Cox model
sections.text:
The Cox proportional hazards model writes h(t | X) = h₀(t) exp(β₁X₁ + ... + βpXp). The baseline hazard h₀(t) is left unspecified. A coefficient β is a log hazard ratio; exp(β) is the hazard ratio for a one-unit increase in X, assumed constant over time.

For example, β = 0.693 gives HR = exp(0.693) ≈ 2.00, so the hazard doubles.

sections.heading: Checking the model
sections.text:
Check proportional hazards with Schoenfeld residuals, a log-minus-log plot (parallel curves if the assumption holds), or time interaction terms. Use martingale and deviance residuals to find poor fit and outliers, and dfbeta or score residuals for influential observations.

Report hazard ratios with confidence intervals, state the time scale and censoring, and remember that association is not causation.

keyPoints: Right censoring means the event time is only known to exceed the observed time.
Survival is S(t)=P(T>t), hazard h(t) is the immediate event rate among those still at risk, and S(t)=exp(−H(t)).
Kaplan-Meier: S_hat(t)=∏(1−d_i/n_i) over event times up to t.
The log-rank test compares survival curves under a null of equal survival.
Cox model: h(t|X)=h0(t)exp(βX), and HR=exp(β) is constant if proportional hazards holds.
Check proportional hazards with Schoenfeld residuals and log-minus-log plots.

en.title: Causal inference from observational studies
en.short: Causal estimands, confounding, matching, propensity scores, sensitivity analysis and limits.

sections.heading: Estimands and confounding
sections.text: A causal estimand is the quantity we want, such as the average treatment effect (ATE): the mean difference between the outcome if everyone were treated and the outcome if everyone were untreated. Each person has two potential outcomes, but we observe only one. Confounding occurs when a variable affects both treatment and outcome, so treated and untreated groups differ before treatment. Adjustment aims for exchangeability: after conditioning on confounders, treatment is as if randomly assigned. Positivity is also needed: every confounder pattern must include both treated and untreated people.

sections.heading: Matching and stratification
sections.text: Matching pairs treated and untreated people with similar confounders; stratification compares treated and untreated within strata of confounders. Both estimate an adjusted difference. Example: 200 people, 100 treated. Crude means: treated 76, untreated 59, difference 17. Within two age strata: young, treated 60 (n=20), untreated 55 (n=80), difference 5; older, treated 80 (n=80), untreated 75 (n=20), difference 5. Stratified ATE = (100/200)×5 + (100/200)×5 = 5. The crude 17 was confounded by age.

sections.heading: Propensity scores
sections.text: A propensity score is the probability of treatment given observed confounders: e(X) = P(T = 1 | X). It is usually estimated by logistic regression. Matching or stratifying on e(X) can balance many confounders at once. It does not remove unmeasured confounding. The score is an adjustment tool, not a causal proof.

sections.heading: Sensitivity and limits
sections.text: Sensitivity analysis asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to change the conclusion. It reports a bias factor or a threshold, not proof that none exists. Observational causal claims are limited by unmeasured confounding, measurement error, selection, and model assumptions. Randomisation remains the strongest design; observational evidence is strongest when several designs and data sources agree.

keyPoints: A causal effect compares potential outcomes; the ATE is E[Y(1) − Y(0)].
Confounding arises when a variable affects both treatment and outcome; adjustment targets exchangeability.
Standardisation estimates the ATE as Σ over strata of (N_s ÷ N) × (mean treated_s − mean untreated_s).
The propensity score is e(X) = P(T = 1 | X); matching or stratifying on it can balance observed confounders.
Sensitivity analysis quantifies how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to overturn a result.
Observational data cannot by themselves prove causation; unmeasured confounding and model assumptions limit claims.

en.title: Mathematical statistics: estimation and testing theory
en.short: Sufficiency, likelihood, exponential families, estimators, Cramer-Rao bound and likelihood ratio tests.

sections.heading: Sufficiency and likelihood
sections.text:
A statistic T(X) is sufficient for a parameter θ if the conditional distribution of the data given T does not depend on θ. The factorisation theorem says the likelihood f(x;θ) equals g(T(x);θ)h(x). The factorisation theorem is the usual way to prove sufficiency.

The likelihood L(θ) is the joint density or probability of the observed data viewed as a function of θ. Ratios of likelihoods compare support for parameter values.

sections.heading: Exponential families
sections.text:
An exponential family has density or mass function f(x;θ)=h(x)exp(Σ a_i(θ)t_i(x)−c(θ)). The functions a_i(θ) are natural parameters. The t_i are sufficient statistics.

Many common models, such as Bernoulli, Poisson and normal with known variance, belong to this family. Their log-likelihood is concave in natural parameters, which helps maximise it.

sections.heading: Estimation and bound
sections.text:
Method of moments sets sample moments equal to population moments and solves for θ. Maximum likelihood chooses θ that maximises L(θ), often by solving the score equation ∂ℓ/∂θ=0, where ℓ=log L. Under regularity, the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal.

The Cramer-Rao bound says any unbiased estimator has variance at least 1/I(θ), where I(θ)=E[(∂ℓ/∂θ)²] is Fisher information. In regular models the MLE attains the bound asymptotically.

Example: for Bernoulli data with n=10 and Σx=4, MLE p̂=0.4. Fisher information per observation is 1/[p(1−p)], so at p=0.4 the bound for p̂ is p(1−p)/n=0.24/10=0.024.

sections.heading: Testing theory
sections.text:
Neyman-Pearson lemma: for simple H0 versus simple H1, the most powerful test rejects H0 when the likelihood ratio L(θ1)/L(θ0) exceeds a constant chosen to give size α. The test is most powerful at the chosen size.

Likelihood ratio tests generalise this to composite hypotheses using Λ=sup_{θ∈Θ0}L(θ) ÷ sup_{θ∈Θ}L(θ); reject for small Λ. Under regularity, −2 log Λ is approximately chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in parameter dimensions.

keyPoints: A sufficient statistic captures all information about the parameter; use the factorisation theorem to find one.
An exponential family has density h(x)exp(Σ a_i(θ)t_i(x)−c(θ)), with sufficient statistics t_i(x).
Method of moments matches sample and population moments; maximum likelihood maximises L(θ), often via the score equation.
Cramer-Rao: for unbiased estimators, Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ), where I(θ) is Fisher information.
Neyman-Pearson: the most powerful simple-versus-simple test rejects for large L(θ1)/L(θ0).
A likelihood ratio test rejects for small Λ = sup under H0 L ÷ sup under full model; −2 log Λ is approximately chi-square under regularity.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and communication in statistics
en.short: Roles, data ethics, reproducible reporting, uncertainty and misleading claims in statistical practice.

sections.heading: Roles and duties
sections.text: Statisticians design studies, manage and analyse data, interpret results and report them. They owe duties to research subjects, clients, employers and the public. Work within your competence and record decisions and assumptions. In consultancy, agree the question, scope, fee, deadlines and data ownership before work starts. Protect independence: a client may want a favourable answer, but the statistician must report what the data support and state limits. Professional codes, such as the American Statistical Association’s Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice and the International Statistical Institute’s Declaration on Professional Ethics, set out these duties; national bodies may add their own.

sections.heading: Privacy and ethics
sections.text: Data privacy is people’s control over their personal information; confidentiality is the duty not to disclose it. Ethical practice needs a lawful basis, informed consent where required, data minimisation, secure storage, limited retention and controlled access. Anonymisation removes identifiers; pseudonymisation replaces them with codes. Neither guarantees safety: small groups and linked datasets can allow re-identification. Laws differ by country. For example, Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) impose duties on personal data. Check current law and your ethics committee.

sections.heading: Reproducible reporting
sections.text: Reproducible reporting means another person can obtain the same results from the same data and code. Report data sources, cleaning rules, model specification, software versions, random seeds and sensitivity analyses. Keep an audit trail. Do not hide failed analyses or report only significant results, which is p-hacking. A report should let a reader judge assumptions and repeat the work.

sections.heading: Communicating results
sections.text: Give estimates with uncertainty, not point estimates. Say 'support was 42%, with a 95% confidence interval from 38% to 46%', not 'support was 42%'. Explain what the interval means and avoid false precision. Graphs can mislead: a truncated y-axis exaggerates change; unequal area scaling and 3D effects distort; dual axes invite false comparisons. Claims can mislead through correlation presented as causation, base-rate neglect (ignoring the underlying rate in the population), or relative risk without absolute risk. State assumptions and practical significance.

keyPoints: Statisticians owe duties to subjects, clients, employers and the public, and must work within their competence.
Privacy laws and ethics rules vary by country; check the current law and ethics approval before handling personal data.
Anonymisation and pseudonymisation reduce but do not remove re-identification risk.
Reproducible reporting gives data sources, cleaning steps, model specification, software versions, seeds and all results.
Communicate uncertainty with confidence intervals or margins of error and plain language, not bare point estimates.
Truncated axes, area scaling, dual axes, correlation-as-causation and relative risk without absolute risk can mislead.

en.title: Advanced statistical inference
en.short: Measure theory, convergence, asymptotic normality, delta method, decision theory, exponential families, U-statistics.

sections.heading: Measure and convergence
sections.text: Measure-theoretic probability puts a probability P on a sigma-field F of subsets of a sample space Ω, giving (Ω,F,P). A random variable is a measurable function from Ω to the real line. Convergence has several modes: in probability, almost surely, in distribution and in Lp. Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution; the reverse implications need extra conditions. These distinctions matter because laws of large numbers and central limit theorems use different modes.

sections.heading: Asymptotic normality
sections.text: An estimator θhat is asymptotically normal when √n(θhat − θ) converges in distribution to N(0, σ²). The delta method transfers this to g(θhat): if g is differentiable at θ and g′(θ) ≠ 0, then √n(g(θhat) − g(θ)) →d N(0, σ²[g′(θ)]²). Example: if Xbar is approximately N(2, 9/100) and g(x)=x², then g′(2)=4 and the variance is 9 × 16 ÷ 100 = 1.44, so Xbar² is approximately N(4, 1.44).

sections.heading: Decision theory
sections.text: Decision theory treats estimation as a choice among actions a under a loss L(θ,a). The risk of a decision rule δ is R(θ,δ)=Eθ[L(θ,δ(X))]. A minimax rule minimises the maximum risk over θ. A Bayes rule minimises the prior-averaged risk for a stated prior. Admissibility asks whether another rule has risk no larger everywhere and smaller somewhere. These criteria can disagree, so no single rule is best for every purpose.

sections.heading: Families and U-statistics
sections.text: An exponential family has density h(x) exp(η(θ)·T(x) − A(θ)). T is a sufficient statistic, and in natural form E[T]=∇A and Cov(T)=∇²A. U-statistics average a symmetric kernel h over all m-subsets: U_n = average h(X_i1,...,X_im). They are unbiased for θ=E[h(X1,...,Xm)]. Under finite variance, √n(U_n−θ) →d N(0, m²ζ1), where ζ1=Var(h1(X1))>0 and h1(x)=E[h(x,X2,...,Xm)]−θ. Under regularity, efficiency compares the variance of an unbiased estimator with the Cramér-Rao bound, 1/(nI(θ)) for n observations, where I(θ) is the Fisher information; an estimator is asymptotically efficient if √n(θhat−θ) reaches variance 1/I(θ) in the limit.

keyPoints: Probability is defined on a probability space (Ω,F,P), and a random variable is a measurable function on Ω.
Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution, but the reverse implications need extra conditions.
Asymptotic normality means √n(θhat − θ) →d N(0, σ²).
The delta method gives √n(g(θhat) − g(θ)) →d N(0, σ²[g′(θ)]²) when g′(θ) ≠ 0.
Risk is R(θ,δ)=Eθ[L(θ,δ(X))]; minimax rules control maximum risk and Bayes rules minimise prior-averaged risk.
For exponential families E[T]=∇A and Cov(T)=∇²A, while a U-statistic of order m has asymptotic variance m²ζ1/n and the Cramér-Rao bound for n observations is 1/(nI(θ)).

en.title: Statistical learning: flexibility, validation and prediction
en.short: Bias-variance, regularisation, cross-validation, trees, ensembles, SVMs, neural networks and high-dimensional selection.

sections.heading: Bias and variance
sections.text:
Statistical learning chooses a model that predicts well on new data, not just on the training sample. Expected squared prediction error splits into bias² + variance + irreducible error. Flexible models have low bias and high variance; rigid models have high bias and low variance: the bias-variance trade-off.

Example: bias = 2, variance = 5, irreducible error = 1 gives 4 + 5 + 1 = 10. A more flexible model with bias = 1 and variance = 9 gives 1 + 9 + 1 = 11, so it is worse.

sections.heading: Regularisation and validation
sections.text:
Regularisation adds a penalty to the loss to shrink coefficients. Ridge minimises RSS + λΣβ², where RSS is the residual sum of squares; lasso minimises RSS + λΣ|β| and can set coefficients to zero. The penalty λ is chosen by cross-validation: split the training data into k folds, fit on k − 1 folds, predict the held-out fold, and average the errors.

For one standardised predictor, ridge gives β̂ = Σxy ÷ (Σx² + λ). If Σx² = 10, Σxy = 8 and λ = 2, β̂ = 8 ÷ 12 = 0.667; λ = 0 gives 0.8.

sections.heading: Trees and kernels
sections.text: A decision tree splits the feature space by thresholds. Deep trees overfit. Bagging averages many trees, as in a random forest, to reduce variance. Boosting fits trees in sequence, each correcting earlier errors, to reduce bias.
