A support vector machine finds the hyperplane with the largest margin between classes; the kernel trick lets it handle non-linear boundaries.

sections.heading: Networks and selection
sections.text: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums and non-linear activation functions. It is trained by backpropagation and gradient descent. With many parameters it needs regularisation and validation. In high dimensions, where predictors p are many relative to observations n, use penalised methods such as lasso, ridge or elastic net (which combines the two penalties), dimension reduction, or sample splitting. Do not select variables and assess error on the same data.

keyPoints: Expected squared prediction error = bias² + variance + irreducible error.
Ridge minimises RSS + λΣβ²; lasso minimises RSS + λΣ|β| and can set coefficients to zero.
For one standardised predictor, ridge β̂ = Σxy ÷ (Σx² + λ).
Cross-validation estimates out-of-sample error by fitting on k − 1 folds and predicting the held-out fold.
Bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias, and an SVM maximises the margin between classes.
Neural networks are trained by backpropagation and need regularisation and validation; in high dimensions avoid selecting and assessing on the same data.

en.title: Hierarchical and mixed-effects models
en.short: Random effects, multilevel and generalised linear mixed models, Bayesian hierarchies, MCMC, checking and prediction.

sections.heading: Random effects
sections.text:
Hierarchical data are grouped: pupils within schools, repeated visits within patients. A random effect is a group-level term drawn from a distribution. A multilevel model combines fixed effects, shared by all groups, with random effects that vary by group.

In a random-intercept model, y_ij = β0 + u_j + e_ij, where u_j ~ N(0, σ_u²) and e_ij ~ N(0, σ_e²). The intraclass correlation is ICC = σ_u² ÷ (σ_u² + σ_e²). If σ_u² = 4 and σ_e² = 16, ICC = 4 ÷ 20 = 0.2: 20% of variance is between groups. Mixed-effects models contain both fixed and random effects.

sections.heading: GLMMs
sections.text: A generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) adds random effects to a generalised linear model. A link function connects the mean to the linear predictor: g(E[y_ij | u_j]) = x_ij′β + z_ij′u_j. For binary data, logit(p_ij) = β0 + u_j. Coefficients describe a typical group, not a marginal average. Fitting by maximum likelihood needs numerical integration or approximation, such as Laplace approximation.

sections.heading: Bayesian hierarchies and MCMC
sections.text: Bayesian hierarchical modelling puts priors on fixed effects and on variance components, for example β ~ N(0, 100²) and σ_u ~ half-normal. The posterior is proportional to likelihood × prior. MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) draws samples from it. Gibbs sampling updates each parameter from its conditional distribution; Metropolis-Hastings and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo handle harder cases. Check chains with trace plots, Rhat near 1 and effective sample size.

sections.heading: Checking and prediction
sections.text: Model checking uses posterior predictive checks: simulate data from the fitted model and compare with observed data. Residual plots reveal misfit. Predictive criteria such as WAIC (widely applicable information criterion) and LOO (leave-one-out cross-validation) help compare models, but they are approximations. Prediction combines fixed effects with estimated random effects. For an existing group, use its conditional mode or BLUP (best linear unbiased predictor). For a new group, set its random effect to zero or average over the random-effect distribution.

keyPoints: A random effect is a group-level term drawn from a distribution; a mixed-effects model has fixed and random effects.
Random-intercept model: y_ij = β0 + u_j + e_ij, with ICC = σ_u² ÷ (σ_u² + σ_e²).
A GLMM applies a link function to a linear predictor containing fixed and random effects.
Bayesian hierarchical models place priors on coefficients and variance components and fit by MCMC.
Check MCMC with trace plots, Rhat near 1 and effective sample size; check fit with posterior predictive checks.
Predict for a new group by setting its random effect to zero or integrating over the random-effect distribution.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in statistics
en.short: From a testable statistical question to a reproducible, ethical dissertation and its defence.

sections.heading: Research question
sections.text: A statistical research question names the population, the variables, and the comparison or relationship to be estimated. It must be answerable with data, specific enough to guide design, and feasible within time and resources. Avoid vague aims such as 'study poverty'; ask instead whether a cash transfer changes household consumption in a named district. State the target parameter, such as a mean difference or odds ratio, and the intended inference.

sections.heading: Review and design
sections.text:
A literature review is a structured search and critical synthesis, not a list of papers. Define search terms, databases, inclusion criteria and dates; record the process so it can be repeated. The review should identify what is known, where methods disagree, and the gap your study addresses.

Design and power follow from the question. Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a stated size if it exists; it rises with sample size, larger effects and lower variability. Do a sample-size calculation before collecting data, using a pilot or published estimates, and report assumptions. Example: a student compares mean exam scores in two groups after a training programme. She states the effect size, estimates variability from a pilot, sets power and significance, then calculates the required number per group. If estimates are uncertain, she reports a range and checks sensitivity.

sections.heading: Reproducible work
sections.text: Reproducible analysis means another person can obtain the same results from the same data and code. Keep raw data unchanged, write a codebook defining every variable and unit, and use scripts rather than manual edits. Store files with version control, document software versions, and back up data securely. Data management plans should cover naming, access, retention and sharing. Requirements vary by country and institution; check your funder and ethics committee.

sections.heading: Ethics and defence
sections.text: Seek ethics approval before data collection; obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality, and avoid plagiarism and gift authorship. Write the dissertation as a clear argument: question, methods, results, limitations. In the defence, explain choices and admit limits calmly.

keyPoints: A good research question names the population, variables and target parameter.
A literature review is a reproducible search and synthesis that identifies the gap.
Power is 1 − β, where β is the probability of a Type II error.
Calculate sample size before data collection and report all assumptions.
Reproducible analysis needs unchanged raw data, a codebook, scripts, version control and secure backup.
Get ethics approval, obtain informed consent, and defend the dissertation honestly, including its limitations.
